Throughout the presidential election campaign of 1992, Candidate 
Chnton was strongly critical of the Reagan-Bush approach to regulation. 
As president, however, he implemented a redesign of regulatory oversight 
that owed a great deal to his predecessors. Exec. Order No. 12,866, 
Regulatory Planning and Review, 58 Fed. Reg. 51735 (1993), reprinted, as 
amended, in Appendix F, below. Intriguingly, despite obvious differences 
regarding substantive regulatory policy, Clinton’s successor, George W. 
Bush, amended the Chnton executive order very little, chiefly to vest 
functions that Clinton had assigned to the vice president instead in the 
president’s chief of staff or in the Director of the Office of Management and 
Budget (0MB). Exec. Order No. 13,258, 67 Fed. Reg. 9385 (2002). See also 
Exec. Order No. 13,422, 72 Fed. Reg. 2763 (2007). The Bush 43 
Administration rehed more on internal directives issued by OMB’s Office 
of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA) to shift the direction of 
federal regulatory pohcy.
President Obama likewise left the Chnton review system substantiahy 
in place, even revoking some of the arguably minor changes imposed by 
George W. Bush. His formal contributions to the system consisted of two 
complementary orders. One executive order reaffirms, but expands upon 
the regulatory philosophy expressed in the Chnton order and directs 
agencies to conduct a retrospective analysis of existing rules to achieve 
consistency with this philosophy. Exec. Order No. 13,563, Improving 
Regulation and Regulatory Review, 76 Fed. Reg. 3,821 (2011). A second 
order exhorts independent agencies to fohow the Chnton-Obama 
principles, and likewise cahs for the submission of plans for those agencies 
to engage in retrospective analysis of the effectiveness of existing rules. 
Exec. Order No. 13,579, Regulation and Independent Regulatory Agencies, 
76 Fed. Reg. 41,587 (2011). Although many readers of Executive Order 
13,563 might weh think its principles reasonably imphcit (or even exphcit) 
in Executive Order 12,866, Professor Cass Sunstein, who headed OIRA 
during most of the first Obama Administration, attributed greater 
significance to it, calling it “a document of signal importance in the Obama 
Administration, indeed a kind of mini-constitution for the regulatory 
state.” Cass R. Sunstein, The Office ofinformation and Regulatory Affairs: 
Myths and Realities, 126 Ha r v . L. REV. 1838, 1845 (2013).
Ah presidential regulatory oversight programs since the Reagan 
Administration have vested a key managerial role in 0MB. As its name 
imphes, 0MB is a bureaucracy atop the bureaucracy, whose role is to help 
the president to budget and manage the executive branch. The director of 
0MB, in turn, uses OIRA to coordinate implementation of presidential 
regulatory oversight. Congress created OIRA to implement the Paperwork 
Reduction Act of 1980, and the 0MB Director determined in 1981 that the
